source.id: TITLE:Language models can explain neurons in language models
source.title: Language models can explain neurons in language models
source.authors: Steven Bills; Nick Cammarata; Dan Mossing; Henk Tillman; Leo Gao; Gabriel Goh; Ilya Sutskever; Jan Leike; Jeff Wu; William Saunders

record.file_problem: none; the text is a flattened web version of the paper. Figures are missing, so plot-only results are not available.
record.tranche_reason: The paper's own results show that most GPT-2 neuron explanations score poorly. It also shows that explanations built from top-activating examples are often too broad and miss where the neuron fires. These bear on V6 and V7.
record.gate_note: Not rows: the choice of top-activating excerpts for explanation generation, the choice of correlation over ablation scoring, the unigram baselines and the direction-finding method (the paper's own methods). Also not rows: the neuron puzzle results (synthetic neurons) and the sparse-activation-function and training-time results (side experiments). These are mentioned in fits_no_version. The paper is an ORIGINAL SOURCE, so no labels are given.
record.test_reason: This paper is the config's original source for V7 (simulation scoring finds only a small share of GPT-2 XL neurons well explained), so it gets no V7 verdict. Its own results also bear on V6. GPT-4 explanations written from 5 top-activating excerpts are often too broad. 42% of sentences written to match an explanation are false positives, and original explanations score worse on new text. In language models it also bears on V4: explanation scores rise with better explainers and revision, and they depend on the activation function. These results argue that reading neurons from their top activations overstates how much is explained, which puts the paper in T5 against the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right but leaves out the headline. The authors' main conclusion is that GPT-4 can explain and score neurons automatically. Its explanations approach human-contractor scores and improve with stronger explainer and simulator models and with revision, and over 1,000 GPT-2 XL neurons score 0.8 or higher. Even so, both GPT-4 and human explanations score poorly in absolute terms (1.7% of GPT-2 XL neurons above 0.7). The typical neuron appeared quite polysemantic, and explanations from top-activating examples are often too broad. The authors propose changing what is explained (activation functions, directions) and better tools. They caution that the size and depth trends may reflect weaknesses of their method rather than of the neurons.
record.recipe_differences: GPT-2 and GPT-3-series subject models, not Qwen3-32B; automated GPT-4 simulation scoring instead of a manual audit of neuron poles; explanations tested on held-out text excerpts, with distinct documents for explanation and scoring.
record.method_sensitivity: Random-only vs top-and-random scoring changes the share of well-explained neurons: 0.2% vs 1.7% above 0.7. Layer, subject model size, explainer and simulator capability, activation function (ReLU beats GeLU) and activation sparsity all change scores. Simulation scoring misses deficits that ablation scoring shows: a correlation score of 0.9 gives ablation scores of 0.3 or 0.6.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablation scoring: replacing a GPT-2 neuron with its simulated activations, from explanations with correlation score 0.9, recovers only about 0.3 (random-only) or 0.6 (top-and-random) of its effect on outputs, measured against mean ablation. The authors say correlation scoring misses deficits that ablation reveals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations that predict a neuron's activations well can still miss much of its effect on the model's outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimised linear combinations of GPT-2 small layer-10 neurons reach an average top-and-random score of 0.718, against 0.147 for random neurons and 0.061 for random directions. The neurons contributing most are often semantically unrelated, and many neurons are needed to recover the score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some directions spread across many neurons are more explainable than single neurons.

record.code_released: Stated as open-sourced (code for explanation and scoring, dataset of explanations, neuron viewer); no URL in the supplied text, only a 'here' link.
record.problems: Most results are shown only in figures. Per-neuron scores are noisy, especially random-only. Explanation and scoring excerpts were not explicitly checked for overlap (footnote 3). The authors say trends may reflect weaknesses of their method. Subject models are old, small GPT models. The puzzle results use synthetic neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Layer-by-layer plots, the unigram baselines, the next-token explanations, the direction-finding results, the training-time and activation-function trends and the human-versus-simulator agreement. All were figure-only or about the paper's own methods and not directly about the claim.

untested.parts: Not tested. There is no Qwen3-32B audit; the paper studies GPT-2 and GPT-3-series models with simulation scoring.

No inspection-based share of one-job neurons in any model. The only bearing is the impression that the typical GPT-2 neuron 'appeared quite polysemantic', with no count (see missing). Simulation-score shares are V7's measure. No mixture-of-experts or trillion-scale models.

No vision models and none of the canonical polysemantic neurons. One GPT-2 neuron ('over and over again' plus repeated items) is speculatively linked to a shared repetition feature, which is not a test.

Vision models and the InceptionV1/ConvNeXt estimates (5% to 99%) are not covered. Neither is regularization, residual or LayerNorm changes, or modern language-model architectures such as SwiGLU. The activation-function tests use ~3M models only.
Not tested. There are no attribution graphs or neuron-level circuits.

Modern models are not covered, nor expert or agent audits, nor explanations that were already tested on written or held-out examples, as in the essay's audit. The explainer is GPT-4 working from 5 top excerpts in a single pass.
This paper is the original source of V7, so it gets no verdict.

missing.what: Activation-function experiments in ~3M models trained from scratch. Activation density was 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001. Sparser activations consistently raise explanation scores but hurt pre-training loss: 0.1 density is about 8.5% and 0.01 about 40% less parameter-efficient. ReLU consistently scores above GeLU. These bear on V4 (architecture, and the cost the version says is absent); the record put them in fits_no_version only.
missing.locator: Subject model trends: Subject model activation function; footnote 27

missing.what: Tool-dependence of scores and late-layer messiness. Scores generally fall in later layers. Next-token explanations work better for a subset of late-layer neurons and match the baseline on average in the last few layers. The authors say the size and depth trends may mostly reflect limits of their method. Scores rise with explainer capability and with revision. Puzzles suggest the explainer, not the scorer, is the bottleneck: the ground truth ranked top in 16 of 19.
missing.locator: Results (layer trend); Next-token-based explanations; Subject model size (last paragraph); Explainer model scaling trends; Revising explanations; Explaining constructed puzzles

missing.what: Human-contractor explanations were written from scratch by non-experts using the same 5 top-activating excerpts. They beat GPT-4 'not by a huge margin' but are 'low in absolute terms'. This is the closest the paper gets to an inspection-based explanation tested on where the neuron fires. It is currently merged into R6, which is linked to V7, and should be its own row.
missing.locator: Assistant model trends: Explainer model scaling trends (paragraph after the first figure)

missing.what: The authors' qualitative impression that the 'typical neuron appeared quite polysemantic' and that 'many of the neurons we inspected were polysemantic', in GPT-2 (XL). No count or method is given. A researcher comparing GPT-2 XL readings would need it, because the essay reports about 70% one-thing neurons for the same model. It is not used for a verdict because it is an impression, not a measurement.

record.verdict_notes:
I read the whole text, which is a flattened web paper with figures missing. The config lists this paper as the original source of V7 only, so V7 rows are linked but get no label.

- **V6** is supported in GPT-2 by R9 to R12. Revision using generated counterexamples improves scores on both sets, but the revised explanations are often too narrow and gains on random-only scoring are limited. That matters when comparing with the essay's audit, which already tests explanations on newly written examples and near misses.
- **V4** labels rest on text the rows do not capture (see missing). The setting is language models with simulation scores, not the essay's vision estimates.
- **R13 (puzzles)** and **R8 (ablation)** are moved off V6. R13 measures the study's own method on synthetic neurons; R8 is a different construct.
- **V3:** one anecdote, the 'over and over again' neuron, is speculatively tied by the authors to a shared repetition feature. It loosely echoes the essay's recursive-generalization idea but is not a test.
- **Independence:** Cammarata (the essay's author) and Gao (author of the main LW challenge) are both core contributors here.
- No instructions were found in the text.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on V6 and V4 (and V7 as original).

tranche.reason: Original source of V7. Its results (generated-sentence false positives, low absolute scores) argue that inspection-based 'one main job' readings need restating.

source_check.notes: Most numerical results are figure-only. R10's role 'control' is wrong (it comes from the revision_rand follow-up). Both V4 verdicts rest on text, not rows. The authors caution that the layer and size trends may reflect their method's limits. The revision experiment partly covers explanations refined on written examples. It is unclear whether this paper is also a V6 original source: V6.support[0] treats it as one, but the test_reason names it as original for V7 only.

statements.problem: The text never studies regularization; the quoted untested line is from the record, not the text. Top-k activation sparsity is architecture, not regularization, so the claim holds.
Text never mentions SwiGLU (GeGLU only in footnote 15); subjects are GPT-2 and GPT-3-series up to 6.7B, so the claim holds for this study.

statements.correction: Next-token explanations do better on a subset of neurons, mostly in later layers, and score about the same as baseline on average in the last few layers. The authors say the layer and size trends 'may be artificial', mostly reflecting limits of their technique. They say the next-token results 'lend credence' to the hypothesis that later-layer neurons are understandable but hard for current methods (lines 648-650).
statements.problem: Cites OpenAI's next-token result against the 'weak tools' phrase, but the authors read that result the other way, as evidence that late-layer neurons are understandable and that current tools are too weak.

statements.correction: The 42% / 86% figures apply to original, unrevised explanations. In the revision experiment, GPT-4 revises each explanation using real activations on 5 GPT-4-written sentences. Original and revised explanations are then scored on the original set and on a set augmented with 5 held-out written sentences. Revised explanations score better on both sets (figure only) but are often too narrow. revision_rand (random nonzero sentences) improves scores almost as much. There are no expert or agent audits.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but differences_stated says Bills does not cover explanations already tested on written examples. The paper's revision experiment does exactly that, with automated GPT-4 revision rather than expert or agent audits.

statements.correction: Bills revises explanations with GPT-4 using activations on 5 GPT-4-written sentences and scores them on held-out written sentences. Revised explanations score better on both the original and augmented sets but are often too narrow. Subjects are GPT-2 only (GPT-3-series up to 6.7B for size trends). There are no expert or agent audits and no recall measure on natural text.
statements.problem: The main untested claim holds for this study: no 10-100B subject, no expert or agent audit, no independent Qwen3-32B test. But the basis says Bills covers no explanations already tested on written examples, and its revision experiment does test such explanations.
0.8 appears only in the Introduction; 0.7 and 0.9 in Results.
Says nothing specific to this study beyond its being the original.
0.3/0.6 are average ablation scores at correlation score 0.9. The 'recover ... of a neuron's effect' wording is loose but acceptable.
